title: I am Joseph (Genesis 45)
hookLine: he weeps so loudly all Egypt hears, and forgives
tomorrow: you thought evil, God turned it to good

cards: Judah has just finished speaking. He's begged to be a slave so the boy can go home to their old father. The room is silent.

And the governor of Egypt, the man wearing Pharaoh's ring, can't hold it anymore. He orders every Egyptian out, even the interpreter. Then, alone with eleven frightened men from Canaan, he starts to cry.
Not quietly. He wept so loud, the text says, that the Egyptians outside heard, and word reached Pharaoh's house. The brothers stand there, waiting for a sentence, and hear that instead.

teach.b: Then two words in Hebrew, three in English: "I am Joseph."

teach.h: I AM JOSEPH. IS MY FATHER ALIVE?
teach.b: And straight after, a question: is my father still alive? The brothers can't answer. They were terrified at his presence, the text says.

Of course they were: the boy they sold now decides whether they eat or starve. So Joseph says, come close. They come, and he says it again, more fully: I am Joseph, your brother, the one you sold into Egypt.

He doesn't pretend it didn't happen; he names it, out loud. Then he says what no one in that room expected: don't be grieved, don't be angry with yourselves. God sent me ahead of you to keep you alive.

teach.h: NOT YOU, BUT GOD, SENT ME HERE.
teach.b: It wasn't you who sent me here, but God. He doesn't erase what they did. He sets it inside something larger.

Then he falls on Benjamin's neck and weeps, and kisses all his brothers, one by one. And a line that's easy to miss: after that, his brothers talked with him. Years of silence, and now they're just talking.
Last, a small human detail as he loads their donkeys with Egyptian gifts and sends them home for Jacob: don't quarrel on the way. From a family that once sold a brother.
When the news reaches Jacob, his heart goes numb; he doesn't believe it. Then he sees the wagons Joseph sent, and he says: Joseph my son is still alive; I'll go and see him before I die.

how: In the sacrament of reconciliation, Catholics name their sins plainly and hear words of absolution: the wrong is named, and then forgiven.

o: the sold brother who forgives them in tears
the son who stole his twin brother's blessing
the dreamer who ruled Egypt as its Pharaoh

games.q: what happens in the room — tap the pairs.
p: his first words to his brothers

s: Joseph forgave by acting like nothing happened
he says it plainly: I am your brother, the one you sold into Egypt. then he forgives.
the Egyptians outside heard Joseph weeping
he cried so loud that word reached Pharaoh's house.
after he kissed them, his brothers talked with him
a small line that's easy to miss, after years of silence.

games.q: you're Joseph. Judah has just offered himself for Benjamin. your brothers have changed. the Egyptians are all around you. what do you do?
o: keep testing them a little longer.
send everyone out, and tell your brothers who you are.
punish them for what they did years ago.
games.why: he clears the room, weeps so loud all Egypt hears, and says: I am Joseph. the test ends the moment Judah steps forward.

practice: Let a face come to mind, someone who hurt you, maybe long ago, and name what happened silently and plainly, the way Joseph did, without softening it.

Then see if you can loosen your grip on it, even a little; letting go isn't the same as saying it was fine. If you pray, hand the grudge to God for now; if you don't, notice what your hands feel like when they open.

wordCard.voice: Joseph. The brother sold into slavery, now governor of Egypt, who reveals himself in tears and forgives the men who sold him. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: I am Joseph. two words, and the whole story turns.

carryVoice: Your line: I am your brother. He named the wrong, and still drew them close. Day three hundred sixty-five: a whole year of days.
